checks_performed: Read and compared the exact target and draft; used no other source file and no web access.
Re-derived the perfect-matching characterization of 2-factors and both factor-splicing bounds.
Checked the edit-radius inequalities and every nil branch, including disconnected graphs, absence of a 2-factor, component obstructions, and low-degree isolation.
Checked the conditional sublinear-factor reduction, including the connectivity precheck and finite exceptional input sizes.
Re-derived exactly the complete-bipartite edit distance using integer incidence counts and checked the explicit Hamiltonian graph with a triangle factor.
No claim depended on finite enumeration: the draft's reported computational checks were not relied upon, and no checker file was applicable.

claims.claim: Existence of a 2-factor, and an explicit 2-factor when one exists, can be determined in polynomial time.
claims.evidence: If some vertex has degree below two, no 2-factor exists. Otherwise, at a degree-d vertex, every perfect matching of the stated auxiliary graph must match its d−2 private dummies to distinct incidence vertices. Exactly two incidences remain, and their only possible matching edges are the links representing original edges. Thus those links select exactly two original edges at every vertex and form a spanning 2-regular graph. Conversely, a 2-factor matches its selected incidences across original-edge links, while the remaining d−2 incidences can be bijectively matched to the private dummies. The auxiliary graph has polynomial size, and general-graph perfect matching is polynomial-time computable.
claims.search_method: Directly proved both directions of the auxiliary-matching equivalence and bounded the gadget size.
claims.witness: The perfect matching itself translates explicitly into the selected original-edge links, which form the returned 2-factor.

claims.claim: If the 2-factor routine reports that none exists, returning (G,nil) is correct.
claims.evidence: Every Hamiltonian cycle is a spanning 2-regular subgraph, hence a 2-factor. Therefore a graph without a 2-factor is non-Hamiltonian. Returning the unchanged graph has edit distance zero, and nil is correct.
claims.search_method: Checked the implication by contraposition from the definition of a Hamiltonian cycle.

claims.claim: If G has a 2-factor with q cycle components, one can add at most q edges and explicitly obtain a Hamiltonian cycle; if G is connected, at most q−1 additions suffice.
claims.evidence: Removing one witness edge from each factor cycle produces q vertex-disjoint spanning paths. Joining their endpoints cyclically uses q connectors, and only connectors absent from G need be added. For connected G, contract the factor cycles. The resulting quotient is connected, so a current merged cycle D has an original edge xy to some unmerged cycle C. Deleting witness edges xx′ and yy′ and using xy plus x′y′ merges the two cycles; only x′y′ may require addition. Repeating q−1 times gives an explicit Hamiltonian cycle with at most q−1 additions. The deleted edges are removed only from the cycle witness, not from G.
claims.search_method: Audited the endpoint splice construction, its connectivity invariant, and its exact edit count.
claims.witness: The spanning paths joined cyclically certify the q-edge bound; the repeated two-edge cycle splice certifies the connected q−1 bound.

claims.claim: For every fixed real 0<c≤3, Sidestep(Hamiltonian Cycle,dist_e,n/c) is in FP.
claims.evidence: Handle the finitely many n<3 cases exactly. For n≥3, a disconnected G is correctly returned with nil. If connected, compute a 2-factor; absence again certifies nil. Otherwise every factor cycle has at least three vertices, so q≤n/3. The connected splice adds at most q−1≤n/3≤n/c edges and supplies an explicit Hamiltonian cycle. All branches are polynomial, retain the labeled vertex set, and return nil only for a graph proved non-Hamiltonian.
claims.search_method: Checked every algorithmic branch, the small-order cases, and the radius inequality for the full interval 0<c≤3.
claims.witness: The algorithm is connectivity test, 2-factor computation, and connected cycle splicing, with exact handling of n<3.

claims.claim: For arbitrary fixed c>0, the target is polynomially solvable on graphs whose girth is at least c.
claims.evidence: On the promised class, disconnected graphs and graphs without a 2-factor admit the preceding correct nil outputs. If a 2-factor exists and the girth is g≥c, each of its q cycles contains at least g vertices. Hence qg≤n and q≤n/g≤n/c. The general q-connector splice is therefore within the radius and constructs a Hamiltonian cycle. Forests cause no exception because they have no 2-factor.
claims.search_method: Verified the promise interpretation, including acyclic graphs, and derived the component bound from cycle lengths.
claims.witness: A computed 2-factor supplies cycles of length at least the promised girth; their endpoint connectors supply the output cycle.

claims.claim: A general cheap non-Hamiltonicity edit is obtained from a component-count obstruction.
claims.evidence: Given the stated S and partition, deleting all cross-part edges makes H−S have at least p components. If S is empty, p>1 makes H disconnected. If |S|=k>0, removing S from any spanning cycle leaves at most k path components; since that cycle would be a spanning subgraph of H−S, H−S could have at most k components. The condition p>k contradicts Hamiltonicity. Thus whenever the specified deletion set has size at most n/c, it gives a valid nil output within the radius.
claims.search_method: Proved the component inequality separately for empty and nonempty S and checked the deletion set exactly realizes it.
claims.witness: A certificate consists of S, the nonempty parts P_1,…,P_p, and the set of at most n/c cross-part edges to delete.

claims.claim: For every c, any graph with a vertex of degree at most n/c admits a polynomial-time valid nil output within radius n/c.
claims.evidence: Choose a minimum-degree vertex v; the hypothesis ensures deg(v)≤n/c. Delete exactly its incident edges. For n≥2 the resulting graph isolates v and is disconnected, hence non-Hamiltonian, while its distance from G is deg(v)≤n/c. Finding v and deleting its incident edges are polynomial-time operations; the constant-size smaller convention is directly decidable.
claims.search_method: Checked the construction, edit count, non-Hamiltonicity certificate, and small-order qualification.
claims.witness: The isolated vertex v is an explicit certificate that the edited graph is disconnected and non-Hamiltonian.

claims.claim: A sublinear-component 2-factor routine would settle the full target for every fixed c.
claims.evidence: Assume the routine returns a 2-factor whenever one exists and returns at most b(n)=o(n) components on Hamiltonian inputs. First return nil on disconnected or no-2-factor inputs. For fixed c, choose and hard-code N with b(n)−1≤n/c for n≥N; inputs below N can be solved exactly in constant work relative to input size. For n≥N let q be the returned component count. If q−1≤n/c, connected splicing supplies the required nearby Hamiltonian graph. If q−1>n/c, G cannot be Hamiltonian, since Hamiltonicity would imply q−1≤b(n)−1≤n/c; returning (G,nil) is then correct. This covers every input under the stated hypothetical guarantee.
claims.search_method: Checked the quantifiers, added the necessary connectivity precheck, and verified the contrapositive and finite-exception argument.
claims.witness: The observed factor component count q determines either a q−1-edge splice or, when too large, a correct non-Hamiltonicity conclusion from the hypothetical guarantee.

claims.claim: For every c>3, high minimum degree alone cannot guarantee a Hamiltonian graph within n/c edits.
claims.evidence: For c>3 the interval (1/c,(1−1/c)/2) is nonempty. Choose rational α in it and infinitely many compatible n, and set a=αn, b=n−a. Then K_{a,b} has minimum degree a>n/c. In any cyclic ordering, if x,z are the numbers of B-B and A-A adjacencies and y is the number of cross adjacencies, the exact incidence equations 2b=2x+y and 2a=2z+y give x−z=b−a. Thus every spanning cycle needs at least x+z≥b−a missing edges. A cyclic arrangement with each A vertex separating a nonempty B-block has z=0 and exactly b−a missing edges, so the distance to the Hamiltonian graphs is exactly b−a=(1−2α)n>n/c.
claims.search_method: Derived matching lower and upper bounds for the edit distance using exact integer incidence equations.
claims.witness: For rational 1/c<α<(1−1/c)/2 and compatible n, the graph K_{αn,(1−α)n} has both minimum degree and Hamiltonian edit distance strictly greater than n/c.

claims.claim: The n/3 component bound for an arbitrary 2-factor remains tight even under the promise that the graph is Hamiltonian.
claims.evidence: For n=3q with q≥2, let T_i={x_i,y_i,z_i}. Include every triangle edge within each T_i, yielding a 2-factor with q=n/3 components. Also include the cycle x_1,x_2,…,x_q,y_1,…,y_q,z_1,…,z_q,x_1. Consecutive vertices in this order belong to different triples, including at the three block boundaries because q≥2, so these added edges form a Hamiltonian cycle. Thus a Hamiltonian graph can indeed contain an arbitrary available 2-factor attaining n/3 components.
claims.search_method: Constructed the graph explicitly and checked every adjacency of the claimed Hamiltonian cyclic ordering.
claims.witness: The graph on triples T_i containing all triangle edges and the displayed interleaved Hamiltonian cycle.

target_evidence: The exact target universally quantifies over every fixed c>0 and every labeled input graph. The draft gives a complete, correctly certified polynomial-time construction only for 0<c≤3, plus correct promised-subclass results, per-input nil constructions, and a conditional sufficient reduction for larger c. It neither proves the general c>3 case nor disproves it: the complete-bipartite family only blocks a particular high-degree completion strategy, and the triangle-factor family only blocks using an arbitrary 2-factor. The final writeup explicitly says the universal statement remains unresolved for c>3, so its PARTIAL claimed resolution is accurate and does not overclaim coverage.
